content: Dalhousie University and the Nova Scotia Rehabilitation and Arthritis Centre in Canada developed a Wheelchair Skills Test to evaluate the ability of wheelchair users to safely perform essential skills for daily living. This research revealed that many wheelchair users lacked the necessary skills. In 2002, the Wheelchair Skills Training Program was created, incorporating evidence-based principles of motor skill learning and wheelchair techniques. Since then, numerous peer-reviewed studies, including systematic reviews and meta-analyses, have confirmed the safety and effectiveness of this training. The program has expanded to include powered wheelchairs, motorized mobility scooters, and caregivers, in addition to manual wheelchair users. It has reached over 173,000 unique users across 200 countries, with its YouTube channel garnering 269,000 views, highlighting the importance of such resources for wheelchair users. Task-specific training can be delivered by clinical or technical personnel or by dedicated trainers with appropriate competencies. Peer trainers who are experienced wheelchair users themselves offer unique advantages, as they can draw on their lived experiences. Female peer trainers, in particular, can serve as role models for women and girls who use wheelchairs, providing inspiration and success stories. An example of peer training in Kenya demonstrates the impact of such initiatives. In Kenya, a partnership between the Motivation Charitable Trust and Kenyatta National Hospital established a peer training network. Peer trainers visit individuals with spinal cord injuries during their initial rehabilitation, sharing their own experiences and addressing gaps they encountered in their rehabilitation. Once a wheelchair is provided, the trainers teach mobility skills, such as transferring and navigating rough terrain, and address health and rights issues. They also provide ongoing support via phone after discharge. These trainers, who have undergone formal training and mentorship, aim to improve the survival and quality of life of people with spinal cord injuries by promoting health, mobility, and independence. This program has positively impacted discharge rates and empowered both trainers and participants. Training should be tailored to the individual wheelchair user’s needs, considering factors such as the type of wheelchair, environments of use, personal goals, and the ability to perform tasks independently or with assistance. For example, new wheelchair users require more training than experienced users, and those receiving a new type of wheelchair may need task-specific training to adapt to changes like seat height or cushion type. Children should receive developmentally appropriate training as they grow and encounter new environments. Group training can be particularly motivating for children. Users with progressive conditions or older adults experiencing functional decline may require frequent training adjustments. Long-term users facing changes in health or aging may need assistance in modifying their methods or improving their ability to instruct others. Individuals at risk of complications, such as pressure injuries or postural problems, need training to mitigate these risks. Wheelchair users with cognitive impairments may benefit from training delivered in familiar environments, shorter and more frequent sessions, and the involvement of caregivers. Training should also be relevant to the environments in which the wheelchair will be used, with mobility skills practiced in settings that mirror the user’s daily life. Follow-up is an integral part of wheelchair service delivery and should be available to all users for as long as they require a wheelchair. Follow-up involves two components: review and remediation. The review process includes collaboration between the user and service provider to assess how well the wheelchair meets the user’s needs, its condition, and the user’s ability to perform necessary tasks. It also involves evaluating the user’s satisfaction with the wheelchair’s performance. Remediation addresses any identified problems, such as adjustments to the wheelchair or additional training for the user and their assistants. Timely maintenance and repair are critical to ensuring safety, health, and mobility while maximizing the wheelchair’s longevity. Follow-up can be conducted remotely via telehealth methods or in person, depending on the context. For example, in Argentina, a program uses telehealth to bridge the distance between local health workers and wheelchair provision personnel located over 1,800 km away. Local health and social workers, trained in wheelchair provision, conduct home visits to assess users’ needs and provide follow-up. Remote clinical advisors review seating positions and provide guidance on simple remediation actions. This program has reduced wheelchair abandonment and improved outcomes for users. Follow-up should be scheduled routinely or initiated as needed when problems arise. Wheelchair users must know how to access both routine and emergency follow-up services. Processes to identify when follow-up is beneficial should be implemented across health systems and other sectors, such as education and social welfare. All healthcare providers involved in the care of wheelchair users should be able to recognize potential issues and facilitate follow-up.
